content:
For more than 40 years, folks have claimed that drivers who set a candy bar on their hood inside Concord Covered Bridge in Georgia will hear the footsteps of ghost children clamoring for the sweet treat. Drivers, of course, use the bridge by day to make their way between Smyrna and Mableton, but come nightfall, many motorists think twice about crossing this historic span.

Where Is Concord Covered Bridge, Georgia's Most Talked-About Haunted Bridge?

Although it's only 25 minutes outside of Atlanta, like other haunted roads across the country, Concord Covered Bridge feels remote, spanning Nickjack Creek in a forested Cobb County ravine between the two closest towns. The historic wooden bridge is only 16 feet wide, but it stretches roughly 133 feet from end to end, supported by stone abutments and concrete piers. Although it's open to traffic, the bridge is too narrow for more than one car to cross at a time, so you have to take turns crossing in opposite directions.

The Legend of Concord Covered Bridge: What Locals Say Happens After Dark

Legend has it that the spirits haunting the bridge belong to children who died along Nickajack Creek in the 1800s. One ghost is said to be that of a local miller's toddler, who wandered into the adjacent gristmill and was killed in the heavy iron gears, while the spirits of several children who drowned in the creek below the bridge also haunt the span.

Sometime in the 1970s, local high schoolers began trying to bait the ghosts with candy, stopping on the bridge, turning off their lights, and leaving chocolate bars on the hoods of their cars at night. Those who've tried it say they've heard hands patting the sides of the cars and footsteps in the rafters of the bridge. When the lights come back on, the candy is gone. Others have reported hearing bodies splash in the creek or seeing lanterns bobbing in the ruins of the stone mill upstream, cementing Concord Covered Bridge's spot among the most haunted places in the U.S.

The Real History Behind Concord Covered Bridge

The candy bar schtick may be little more than suburban legend, but Nickajack Creek and the area around the bridge have seen plenty of bloodshed and tragedy. According to National Register of Historic Places documents, settlers built a flat-deck bridge on the site to serve a water-powered gristmill, but it was later burned during the Civil War Battle of Ruff's Mill.

After the war, a three-story stone woolen mill was constructed just downstream, and in 1872, the span was rebuilt as a covered bridge on the original stone piers. The bridge was updated and fortified in 1891. Accounts from residents of the Miller's House, which has stood alongside the bridge since the 1850s, say that a child died in the gristmill machinery sometime during the 19th century, and in 1913 two men died in a train derailment from a nearby trestle over the creek. Although they weren't all children, the bridge has seen its share of tragedy.

Why Some Georgia Locals Still Won't Cross Concord Covered Bridge at Night

The reason many drivers avoid crossing Concord Covered Bridge at night has less to do with it being one of the most haunted places in Georgia and more with the fact that the approach is steep and curvy, funneling drivers into a 133-foot-long wooden box designed to carry horse-drawn wagons and not full-sized SUVs. Despite its 13-foot interior height, the entrance to the bridge is only 7 feet high, something folks in taller vehicles may prefer to eyeball in the daylight. In fact, the most frequent cause of road closures at the bridge is oversized vehicles whose drivers either ignore the height restriction or feel overly optimistic about their chances. Throw in the slow-going of cars taking turns to cross and combine it with the chance of running into ghost-hunting teens who've stopped their car in the middle of the bridge and turned off their lights, and the East-West Connector seems like a much better nighttime option.

What To Know Before Driving Concord Covered Bridge

You'll definitely want to add the Concord Covered Bridge Historic District to your must-visit list. Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1980 and maintained by the Friends of the Concord Covered Bridge Historic District, the site preserves the bridge, historic Ruff's Mill, and the Miler's House. Despite being a one-lane bridge that handles two-way traffic, more than 8,000 vehicles a day cross the span, so expect some backup. You'll also want to make sure your vehicle, including any roof racks, will clear the 7-foot cap before entering… and don't stop in the middle with a candy bar. Instead, park at the Silver Comet Trail lot along Concord Road or at Heritage Park on Fontaine Road and use the boardwalk that follows the banks of the creek.

FAQs About Concord Covered Bridge

Is Concord Covered Bridge really haunted?

There's no evidence Concord Covered Bridge is haunted, but its legend has circulated since at least the 1970s, according to Jim Miles's book Weird Georgia. Most stories center on ghost children who take candy left on parked cars. The road's documented history includes an 1864 Civil War battle and a fatal mill accident, which locals believe sparked the lore.

Where is Concord Covered Bridge in Georgia?

Concord Covered Bridge runs about 132 feet across Nickajack Creek along Concord Road in Cobb County, near Smyrna, in northwest Georgia. It's a public paved road with a wooden bridge deck, roughly 25 minutes northwest of downtown Atlanta, and it connects Smyrna on the east side to Mableton on the west.

Can you drive Concord Covered Bridge at night?

Yes, Concord Covered Bridge is a public road open year-round, but it's unlit, narrow, and limited to vehicles no higher than 7 feet. If you go after dark, stay in your vehicle, keep moving with traffic, and don't stop inside the bridge or park on nearby private property.

What is the most haunted road in Georgia?

Concord Covered Bridge is often called the most haunted road in the Atlanta suburbs, a title Georgia folklore guides have given it since the 1980s. Other roads with well-known legends in the state include Seven Bridges Road in Floyd County and Spook Bridge over the Little River near Valdosta.
